name: Primes Sieve
summary: Count and sum the primes up to N and find the largest one, with the Sieve of Eratosthenes.

spec.description: The Sieve of Eratosthenes over one byte per integer. Crossing off multiples is a stream of strided writes over a large array and the final scan reads it sequentially, so this measures tight loops, bounds checks and memory bandwidth.
spec.input: Exactly one argument N made only of ASCII digits (leading zeros allowed), with 0 ≤ N ≤ 200000000.
spec.output: Three lines: count: C, sum: S and largest: P (each followed by \n), where C is the number of primes ≤ N, S their sum (unsigned 64-bit, fits for the allowed range) and P the largest prime ≤ N (0 when there is none). Exit code 0.
rules: One byte (or bool) flag per integer 0..N: no bit packing, no odd-only layout, no wheel, no segmentation.
For p = 2, 3, … while p × p ≤ N: if p is still marked prime, cross off p × p, p × p + p, … ≤ N. Then scan the flags to count, sum and find the largest prime.
Python may cross off with slice assignment and scan with itertools.compress (the idiomatic built-ins for the same algorithm).
Missing or extra arguments, non-digit characters or N > 200000000: usage message on stderr, nothing on stdout, exit code 1.

benchmarks.name: 1 million
benchmarks.description: N = 1,000,000: a 1 MB flag array that fits in cache, so startup and loop overhead dominate.

benchmarks.name: 100 million
benchmarks.description: N = 100,000,000: a 100 MB flag array far larger than any cache; strided writes and the final scan are bound by memory bandwidth.
